title: Fabless Quantum Chip Design and Commercial Production
authors: Cai, Ling Qiao, Bin Yang, Fumin Luo, WeiGui Guo, GuoRong Zhang, XueFei Liu, Qinglang Guo, Bin Wu
abstract: This paper proposes a fabless quantum-chip design and production architecture for superconducting quantum computing, centered on the SPICE-Q multiphysics simulation framework. The proposed ecosystem connects process-certified quantum PDKs, parameterized device cells, traceable model cards, SPICE-Q physical modeling languages, unified Q-EDA flows, foundry sign-off rules, cryogenic test feedback, and reusable quantum IP. In this model, design firms do not merely outsource fabrication; they prepare verified tape-outs under standardized process constraints and calibrated physical models. Its economic value lies in reducing repetitive device debugging, process exploration, and low-level layout effort, while its feasibility depends on PDK maturity, foundry yield, cryogenic test throughput, model-prediction accuracy, data-feedback mechanisms, and IP licensing boundaries. We argue that superconducting quantum chips can move from the current largely vertically integrated development model toward a fabless-foundry ecosystem only when hardware design is supported by standardized, verifiable, and reusable software and process interfaces. The required pillars are certified PDKs, PCell-based parameterized design, SPICE-Q cross-physics simulation, end-to-end Q-EDA automation, and a tradable quantum-IP market. By adapting lessons from the classical semiconductor industry to quantum hardware, this framework defines a path toward scalable, manufacturable, and commercially reusable superconducting quantum-chip design.
summary: This paper outlines a comprehensive fabless architecture necessary to commercialize superconducting quantum chips by mimicking the successful model of the classical semiconductor industry. It argues that moving beyond lab prototypes requires standardizing design through five key pillars: PDKs, parameterized cells, multiphysics simulation (SPICE-Q), automated EDA flows, and an IP market. Ultimately, it defines a path toward scalable, manufacturable quantum hardware by treating physical complexity as a set of verifiable software interfaces.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of transitioning superconducting quantum chip development from a laboratory-based, vertically integrated model to a scalable, standardized fabless-foundry industrial ecosystem.
main_result: Scalability requires establishing five key pillars—PDKs, PCells, SPICE-Q simulation, Q-EDA automation, and a Q-IP market—to create verifiable, reusable software and process interfaces.
method: The authors propose an architectural framework by drawing analogies from the classical semiconductor industry to define necessary industrial standards for quantum hardware design flow.
model_or_system: The physical system is superconducting quantum chips (e.g., Transmons). The model involves a complex, multi-physics Hamiltonian ($H_{SPICE-Q}$) whose performance depends on coupling geometry, material loss, and packaging constraints.
key_observables: Logical error rate, Q-IP reuse rate, cross-foundry process consistency, and the overall system validation maturity ($V_{	ext{validation}}$).
important_parameters: PDK maturity, foundry yield, cryogenic test throughput, and the boundaries of Quantum Intellectual Property (Q-IP) licensing.
main_assumptions: The transition assumes that establishing rigorous, standardized interfaces can overcome the inherent physical complexity and non-ideal nature of quantum devices, allowing for 'constrained decoupling' from full process ownership.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the limitations of the current IDM model, then proposing a multi-pillar fabless architecture (PDKs $ightarrow$ PCells $ightarrow$ SPICE-Q $ightarrow$ Q-EDA $ightarrow$ Q-IP), and finally detailing the required continuous closed-loop feedback mechanisms for industrial maturity.
why_interesting: It provides a crucial engineering roadmap, framing quantum hardware development not just as a physics problem but as an industrial systems integration challenge that requires rigorous standardization analogous to mature classical semiconductor flows.
